Tiszaszalka New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Tiszaszalka, Hungary

Not demolished. The newer of two Jewish cemeteries in Tiszaszalka, established around 1890 and active until at least 1944. Jews settled in the village from the early 19th century (possibly earlier, per Hebrew Wikipedia), working as estate owners, farmers, merchants, artisans, and liquor vendors; population peaked at 144 by 1910. Initially part of the Mezőkaszony Jewish community, Tiszaszalka came under Vásárosnamény's jurisdiction after WWI, maintaining a burial society, a 'Hachnasat Kala' charity for poor brides, and a nursing home. The community briefly split into two synagogues; various rabbis - including Herman Roth and rabbinical court heads Yoel Zvi Rata and Yaakov Ratenberg - led religious life, alongside a butcher-teacher-cantor combining several roles. Antisemitic violence escalated over decades: 1919 Communist-era looting, 1920s 'White Terror' attacks, the unpunished 1937 murder of the village shochet, and a targeted 1939 'citizenship check' resulting in mass arrests. In April 1944, 70 Jews were confined in the synagogue before dawn transport to the Beregszász Ghetto and deportation to Auschwitz in May; the handful of survivors who returned soon left for good.
